title: Common2 membership of FIFO queues
formal:
Is the following proposition true?
\[
\forall n\in\mathbb N,\ n\ge3\quad
\exists A_n:\quad A_n\text{ implements a linearizable wait-free FIFO queue for }n\text{ processes}
\]
using only the atomic read/write registers and one-shot test-and-set bits defined below? The queue is initially empty and has no capacity bound. Every process may perform arbitrarily many operations of either kind, with arbitrary finite binary strings as enqueued values. Each \(A_n\) is deterministic and has finite code; it may depend on \(n\). The quantifiers do not additionally require one compiler producing all \(A_n\).
definitions:
Fix \(n\ge3\). There are \(n\) named sequential processes with identifiers \(1,\ldots,n\), each knowing \(n\) and its own identifier. A process has unbounded private storage, initially containing only its identifier, \(n\), and its fixed program data. Its local computation is given by a deterministic finite Turing program on finite strings. Shared communication is confined to two countable arrays with natural-number addresses: registers \(R_0,R_1,\ldots\), initially containing the empty binary string, and bits \(B_0,B_1,\ldots\), initially zero. A register read atomically returns its whole current finite string; a write atomically replaces that string and returns an acknowledgement. The primitive \(\operatorname{TAS}(j)\) atomically returns the old value of \(B_j\) and changes it to one. A bit is never reset, and every later test-and-set on that bit returns one. Any process can access any address; using a previously unused address does not require an allocation oracle. There is no fixed bound on addresses used, register bit lengths, private storage or total operations over a whole execution. A finite execution prefix uses only finite data and finitely many primitive calls.

The scheduler interleaves individual local computation steps and atomic primitive calls. Each scheduled process chooses its next action from its private state, its current invocation and previous primitive responses. Processes receive no randomness, clock, failure detector, schedule information or noncomputable oracle. They can be delayed arbitrarily and can stop forever at any point. No fairness assumption constrains other processes. Local Turing steps, primitive invocations and operation responses count as that process's own steps; no bounded step complexity is demanded.

The sequential queue state is a finite sequence of finite binary strings, initially empty. \(\operatorname{Enqueue}(v)\) appends one occurrence of \(v\) at the end and returns a distinguished acknowledgement. \(\operatorname{Dequeue}()\) removes and returns the first occurrence if the sequence is nonempty; otherwise it returns a distinguished \(\mathsf{Empty}\) value without changing the state. Empty, acknowledgement and string-valued responses have separate tags, so the empty binary string is an ordinary possible item. Repeated equal values represent separate occurrences. Each process can invoke either operation whenever its previous invocation has returned, so it has at most one pending invocation. Clients may choose later invocations from earlier responses; there are no designated enqueuer or dequeuer roles, no bound on the number of calls and no promise that a dequeue finds an item.

Linearizability is required for every finite execution prefix. Take its history of queue invocations and responses. Append responses to any chosen subset of pending invocations and discard the other pending invocations. There must be a total order of the resulting completed operations that preserves each process's order, respects every real-time precedence in the completed history, and gives exactly their responses under the sequential queue specification. Here real-time precedence means that one operation's response occurs before the other's invocation. The choice of this total order may differ between different execution prefixes; it is not required to preserve earlier choices when a history is extended. Infinite executions must satisfy this safety condition at every finite prefix.

Wait-freedom is the following per-process termination property: from any reachable configuration with a pending operation of process \(p\), every continuation in which \(p\) takes infinitely many of its own steps contains a response to that operation after finitely many such steps, regardless of all other processes' delays, crashes or continuing operations. Thus an infinite execution in which one process's pending operation never finishes despite that process continuing to take steps is forbidden, even if other operations keep completing. These definitions specify ordinary linearizability and wait-freedom, with unlimited resource capacity; they impose neither strong linearizability nor a resource bound uniform over all histories.
why: A queue orders work shared by concurrent processes. This question asks whether very weak synchronization suffices to guarantee that each continuing process finishes, even while others stop or interfere. It tests the distinction between consensus power and the ability to implement a reusable data type.

context_blocks.text: The OPODIS 2015 paper, published in 2016, explicitly asks whether an \(n\)-process ordinary linearizable wait-free queue can be built from test-and-set and registers for every \(n\ge3\). This card retains that quantifier order and the unrestricted repeated-operation interface, with finite-string values and explicit deterministic computation conventions.

The consensus number of an object type is the largest number of processes for which copies of that type together with registers can solve wait-free consensus: every continuing process decides one proposed input value and all decisions agree. Test-and-set and queues have consensus number two. That agreement capability by itself does not supply a many-process queue implementation. Common2 is the historical class of types implementable in a wait-free manner from any object type of consensus number two.

Stacks admit Common2 implementations. This result concerns last-in-first-out removal and does not supply the first-in-first-out semantics of the target. The source also studies unbounded numbers of participating processes; the present question allows a separate implementation for each fixed finite process count.

Eisenstat gives a Common2 queue for at most two enqueuing processes and any number of dequeuing processes. The stated restriction on who can enqueue leaves the unrestricted interface in this card unanswered.

The OPODIS 2022 article, published in February 2023, explicitly repeats the open Common2 queue question. Its efficient exact queue uses compare-and-swap, which atomically checks an expected value and conditionally writes a replacement; that primitive is unavailable here. Its separate multiplicity variant relaxes removal semantics.

Strong linearizability requires one choice of linearizations that preserves prefixes across histories. The 2025 paper proves an impossibility for strongly linearizable queues from the relevant weak primitives. Its progress condition is lock-freedom, meaning that infinitely many steps yield infinitely many completed operations somewhere in the system. The stronger correctness requirement prevents this result from being an impossibility for ordinary linearizability.

The PODC 2026 paper extends impossibility results for strongly linearizable queues, including settings with additional primitives and at least four processes. Those results continue to assume strong linearizability. The checked full version therefore does not refute the ordinary wait-free target.

progress.text: Stacks are shown to belong to Common2; the queue question is kept separate.
The revised preprint provides a queue with two enqueuers and any number of dequeuers.
The published OPODIS 2015 article explicitly states the unrestricted ordinary wait-free queue question.
The published OPODIS 2022 article still identifies Common2 queue membership as open while giving bounds with stronger primitives.
An impossibility theorem excludes strongly linearizable lock-free queues from the stated weak primitives.
The PODC paper extends strong-linearizability impossibilities; the checked full version retains that stronger hypothesis.

answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed proposition, including both safety and per-process termination for every \(n\ge3\), or a complete Lean proof of its logical negation: there is an integer \(n\ge3\) for which no permitted implementation exists. A result confined to restricted process roles, stronger primitives, a stronger correctness condition, or system-wide progress alone does not settle this proposition.
status_note: Explicitly open in the OPODIS 2015 article published in 2016 and again in the OPODIS 2022 article published in February 2023. The bounded source and subsequent-result review on 16 September 2026 found no resolution of the unrestricted ordinary linearizable wait-free queue target. The checked 2025 and 2026 impossibility theorems assume strong linearizability; they are not refutations of this card. This status records dated source evidence, not exhaustive current-openness certification.

statement_review.notes: Retained the original every-fixed-n ordinary linearizable wait-free queue target, without adding uniform compilation across n. Specified finite deterministic local programs, fixed initial shared memory, binary-string values, repeated unrestricted operations, exact prefix safety and per-process termination. Distinguished shared capacity from quantitative space/step bounds, empty queue responses from constant-time claims, and ordinary linearizability from prefix-preserving strong linearizability. Preserved importance 86 and category. Corrected the reference publication year: OPODIS 2015 article 31 was published on 13 October 2016.
statement_review.scope: Individual formulation and source review; current-status limits are recorded separately.

importance.reason: The queue question tests whether consensus number alone captures the strength of basic concurrent data types, and whether weak primitives can provide per-process progress.

category_assignment.reason: The target is concurrent implementability and per-process progress from specified shared-memory primitives.

sentences: Several named processes repeatedly insert arbitrary items into a first-in-first-out queue and remove the oldest remaining item.
Only atomic read/write registers and initially unused test-and-set bits are available, with no fixed memory-capacity limit.
For every fixed process count, the question asks for a deterministic implementation in which every continuing process finishes each operation despite arbitrary interference or crashes.
Correctness requires ordinary linearizability, allowing a legal sequential explanation of every history without demanding one prefix-preserving choice across histories.
Known restricted-role queues and impossibility theorems under strong linearizability do not settle this unrestricted target.
